claims.text: A controlled compositional gradient within the FCC layers will modulate local stacking-fault energy.
Modulation of local stacking-fault energy will promote deformation-twin nucleation during sustained creep loading.
Deformation twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The deformation twins progressively accommodate plastic deformation.
The deformation twins delay the onset of accelerated creep.
The starting multilayers have uniform FCC-layer composition, well-defined layer thicknesses, and well-defined interfaces.
A slight chemical gradient can be introduced into the FCC layers through variable-profile co-sputtering.
High-resolution compositional mapping can verify the intended stacking-fault-energy modulation.
The intended compositional gradient can be produced without compromising phase stability.
Room to moderately elevated creep-test temperatures can favor twin nucleation while preserving the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Severe lattice distortion and inherent short-range order in HEAs lower the energy barrier for twin nucleation.
The imposed compositional gradient increases deformation-twin density by modulating local stacking-fault energies.
Twin-mediated obstruction of dislocations produces a more homogeneous plastic-strain distribution.
Twin-mediated obstruction of dislocations delays rapid creep-strain accumulation.
Relative to a uniform-composition baseline, the graded multilayer will have a higher deformation-twin density.
Relative to the baseline, the graded multilayer will exhibit a more uniform distribution of plastic strain.
Relative to the baseline, the graded multilayer will show a delayed onset of rapid creep-strain accumulation.
The proposed behavior is restricted to a controlled nanoscale multilayer architecture, the studied temperature range, and controlled loading conditions.
